topic: Hip flexor strain in kicking sports

slides.headline: Front of hip grabs when you kick?
slides.sub: A hip flexor strain is common in kicking sports. Here's the road back.

slides.title: Where it usually happens
slides.body: Kicking, sprinting and quick changes of direction load the hip flexors hard, especially when you're tired late in a game. Pain at the front of the hip or top of the thigh is typical.

slides.title: Keep moving, but adjust
slides.body: Complete rest usually slows things down. Walking, cycling or swimming within comfort keep you fit while the strain settles. Pain up to a mild, settling level is usually okay.

slides.title: Load it back up gradually
slides.body: Start with gentle holds like lifting your knee against your hand, then progress to marching, lunges and resisted knee drives. Strength before speed is a good rule.

slides.title: Kicking comes last
slides.body: Build from passing short to long, then shooting, then full-speed kicks. Most people move up a step when the previous one feels easy the next morning.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A pop with sudden pain, trouble walking, a lump or bruising, or groin pain that keeps coming back is worth an assessment rather than playing through it.

slides.headline: Back on the pitch, step by step

caption:
Front of your hip grabbing every time you kick or sprint?

Soccer, footy, touch and Oztag all put big demands on the hip flexors, especially late in a game. A strain usually shows up as pain at the front of the hip or top of the thigh.

Most people do better staying active within comfort, then building strength gradually: gentle holds, then marching and lunges, then resisted drives. Kicking comes last, starting short and slow. A pop, bruising or trouble walking is worth getting assessed.

story.headline: Hip grabs when you kick?
story.body: Swap kicking for a few days of walking or cycling, then start gentle knee lifts against your hand.
